title: Chapter XVI

teacherSummary.text: At Mrs. Phillips's party, Wickham tells Elizabeth that Darcy denied him a clergyman's living promised by Darcy's father. Elizabeth believes him readily.

vocabulary.definition: To lead into a wrong way or path
vocabulary.context: Collins,” said she, “speaks highly both of Lady Catherine and her daughter; but from some particulars that he has related of her ladyship, I suspect his gratitude misleads him, and that in spite of her being his patroness, she is an arrogant, conceited woman.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “mislead”: mis- (Old English mis-, "wrongly"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The condition of being out of favor
vocabulary.context: His behaviour to myself has been scandalous; but I verily believe I could forgive him anything and everything, rather than his disappointing the hopes and disgracing the memory of his father.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “disgrace”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To turn back, or to the contrary
vocabulary.context: After many pauses and many trials of other subjects, Elizabeth could not help reverting once more to the first, and saying—
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “revert”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + vert (Latin vertere, "to turn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: I have a warm, unguarded temper, and I may perhaps have sometimes spoken my opinion of him, and to him, too freely.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unguard”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + ard (Latin ardere, "to burn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A man who becomes sponsor for a child at baptism, and makes himself a surety for its Christian training and instruction
vocabulary.context: He was my godfather, and excessively attached to me.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “godfather”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To give or leave by will
vocabulary.context: Darcy bequeathed me the next presentation of the best living in his gift.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “bequeath”: be- (Old English be-, "thoroughly, about"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The officers of the ——shire were in general a very creditable, gentleman-like set, and the best of them were of the present party; but Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “creditable”: cred (Latin credere, "to believe") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: One who lives in the same house or apartment with another
vocabulary.context: “We were born in the same parish, within the same park, the greatest part of our youth was passed together; inmates of the same house, sharing the same amusements, objects of the same parental care.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “inmate”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: A military life is not what I was intended for, but circumstances have now made it eligible.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “eligible”: -ible (Latin -ibilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Giving offense to the conscience or moral feelings
vocabulary.context: His behaviour to myself has been scandalous; but I verily believe I could forgive him anything and everything, rather than his disappointing the hopes and disgracing the memory of his father.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain

context.history: A 'living' was a church post with income controlled by a patron.

significance: Readers learn alongside Elizabeth that a confident story is not proof—central to the theme of prejudice.
discussionQuestions: What evidence does Elizabeth have that Wickham is telling the truth?
Where does point of view appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

items.prompt: What does Wickham claim Darcy did?
What theme does Elizabeth's belief show?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XVI,” how does Austen show a persuasive tale? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the point of view you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XVI develops the idea of a persuasive tale. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of point of view and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses point of view in Chapter XVI to complicate the reader's understanding of a persuasive tale. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XVI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a persuasive tale responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XVI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a persuasive tale. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: “It was the prospect of constant society, and good society,” he added, “which was my chief inducement to enter the ——shire. I knew it to be a most respectable, agreeable corps, and my friend Denny tempted me farther by his account of their present quarters, and the very great attentions and excellent acquaintance Meryton had procured them. Society, I own, is necessary to me. I have been a disappointed man, and my spirits will not bear solitude. I must have employment and society. A military life is not what I was intended for, but circumstances have now made it eligible. The church ought to have been my profession—I was brought up for the church, and I should at this time have been in possession of a most valuable living, had it pleased the gentleman we were speaking of just now.”
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XVI”?

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What evidence does Elizabeth have that Wickham is telling the truth? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are misleads, disgracing, reverting, unguarded, godfather. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Collins,” said she, “speaks highly both of Lady Catherine and her daughter; but from some particulars that he has related of her ladyship, I suspect his gratitude misleads him, and that in spite of her being his patroness, she is an arrogant, conceited woman.”” Webster's says: To lead into a wrong way or path. Now the word history: “mislead”: mis- (Old English mis-, "wrongly"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “disgrace”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “revert”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + vert (Latin vertere, "to turn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. A 'living' was a church post with income controlled by a patron. Why does this chapter matter? Readers learn alongside Elizabeth that a confident story is not proof—central to the theme of prejudice. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for point of view.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see point of view, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to a persuasive tale.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Point of view, Irony, Characterization.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of point of view. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
